questions.prompt: What is the main aim of the World Trade Organization (WTO)?

options.text: To set exchange rates between member countries' currencies
options.misconception: Managing currencies is linked to the IMF, not the WTO.

options.text: To lend money to developing countries for infrastructure projects
options.misconception: Development lending is the role of the World Bank, not the WTO.

options.text: To make trade between countries freer by reducing trade barriers
To make sure every member country has a trade surplus
options.misconception: Not every country can have a surplus at the same time, and this is not a WTO goal.

hints: Think about what the WTO does to the rules that govern trade between countries.
Rule out the options that describe other international organizations, then check what is left against the WTO's purpose.
questions.targets: Role of the WTO vs IMF and World Bank

questions.prompt: Define the term economic integration.
marking_points: Co-operation between countries / countries reduce barriers between them and co-ordinate economic policies [1]
leading to closer economic links between them (e.g. more trade, factor movements) [1]
questions.model_answer_note: Full marks for a definition that covers both co-operation or policy co-ordination and the resulting closer economic ties; one of the two earns 1.
hints: This term sits behind every type of trading bloc, from a preferential trade agreement to a monetary union.
Say what the countries do together, and then what happens to the links between their economies as a result.
questions.targets: Core definition for trading bloc questions

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between a free trade area and a customs union?

options.text: Members of a customs union set the same tariffs on imports from non-members
Members of a free trade area share a common currency
options.misconception: Neither a free trade area nor a customs union needs a common currency; that belongs to a monetary union.

options.text: Only a customs union removes tariffs on trade between its members
options.misconception: Both types remove trade barriers between members.

options.text: Members of a customs union allow workers to move freely between them
options.misconception: Free movement of labour is the added feature of a common market, not a customs union.

hints: Put the types of trading bloc in order of how integrated they are.
Ask what one step up from a free trade area adds, especially for trade with countries outside the bloc.
questions.targets: Common external tariff as the feature that separates the two

questions.prompt: Which situation is an example of dumping?

options.text: A Kuvan firm sells its steel in Veld at a price higher than it charges at home
options.misconception: Charging more abroad is the opposite of dumping.

options.text: Veld places a quota on steel imports from Kuva
options.misconception: A quota is a form of protection, not dumping; dumping is done by the exporter.

options.text: A Kuvan firm exports steel to Veld because Kuva has a comparative advantage in steel
options.misconception: Exporting because of comparative advantage is normal trade based on lower opportunity cost.

options.text: A subsidised Kuvan firm sells its steel in Veld at a price below its cost of production

hints: Think about the price at which the exporting firm sells abroad and how it compares with its costs.
Check each option: who is acting, and is the export price fair compared with what it costs to make the good?

questions.prompt: Outline two functions of the World Trade Organization (WTO).
marking_points: One function outlined, e.g. provides a forum for negotiating trade agreements to reduce trade barriers [1]
A second function outlined, e.g. settles trade disputes between members / monitors members' trade policies / enforces trade rules [1]
questions.model_answer_note: Two distinct functions, each briefly outlined, earn 2; a list of two words without any detail earns 1 at most.
hints: Think about what the WTO does before a trade agreement exists and what it does when members disagree.
Write one sentence for each function, saying what the WTO does and why.
questions.targets: WTO functions: negotiation, dispute settlement, monitoring

questions.prompt: Which argument is most often used to justify protecting a newly established domestic industry?

options.text: New domestic firms cannot yet produce at low average costs because they have not reached economies of scale
Imports from abroad are always of lower quality than domestic goods
options.misconception: Import quality is not the basis of this argument and is not always true.

options.text: The industry has been in decline for many years and workers need time to retrain
options.misconception: This describes protecting a declining (sunset) industry, not a new one.

options.text: The good is needed in wartime so the country must never rely on imports
options.misconception: This is the national security (strategic) argument.

hints: This is the infant industry argument.
Think about why a young firm might struggle to compete on price with large, established foreign firms.
questions.targets: Infant industry argument vs other arguments

questions.prompt: Table 1 shows features of four trading blocs. Which bloc is a common market?

table.caption: Table 1: Features of four trading blocs
columns: Free movement of labour and capital

options.text: Bloc W
options.misconception: Bloc W only removes barriers between members, so it is a free trade area.

options.text: Bloc X
options.misconception: Bloc X adds a common external tariff but no factor mobility, so it is a customs union.

options.text: Bloc Y
Bloc Z
options.misconception: Bloc Z also shares a currency, so it has gone beyond a common market to a monetary union.

hints: Use the stages of economic integration and match each stage to its features in Table 1.
Work along each row and find the bloc that has the features of a customs union plus one more, but no shared currency.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an argument against trade protection?

options.text: It protects jobs in domestic industries facing foreign competition
options.misconception: This is one of the main arguments for protection.

options.text: It can reduce a deficit on the balance of trade
options.misconception: This is an argument used in favour of protection.

options.text: It raises prices and reduces choice for domestic consumers
It raises revenue for the government through tariffs
options.misconception: Government revenue is an argument used in favour of tariffs.

hints: Think about who loses when imports become dearer or scarcer.
Sort the options into benefits claimed by supporters of protection and costs pointed out by critics.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a free trade area and a common market.
marking_points: A free trade area removes trade barriers between members, but each member keeps its own trade policy / tariffs towards non-members [1]
A common market has a common external tariff and also allows free movement of factors of production (labour and capital) between members [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full answer gives the feature of each type and makes the contrast clear; describing only one type earns 1.
hints: Place both types on the stages of economic integration and note the stages in between.
State what each type does about non-member trade and about the movement of workers and capital, then contrast them.
questions.targets: Asked as a comparison in past papers

questions.prompt: Which describes a preferential trade agreement?

options.text: Member countries give each other lower trade barriers on certain goods
Member countries adopt a single currency and one central bank
options.misconception: This is a monetary union, the most integrated stage.

options.text: Member countries remove all barriers to trade and set a common external tariff
options.misconception: This describes a customs union.

options.text: Member countries allow free movement of labour and capital
options.misconception: Factor mobility is the feature of a common market.

hints: This is the first, least integrated stage of economic integration.
Look for the option where barriers are reduced for some goods rather than removed on everything.

questions.prompt: Explain the anti-dumping argument for trade protection.
marking_points: Dumping is when a foreign firm sells exports at a price below its cost of production, often helped by a subsidy [1]
This is unfair competition that can drive efficient domestic firms out of the market / cause job losses [1]
So the importing country may impose tariffs or quotas on the dumped goods to limit these imports and protect domestic producers [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full answer explains what dumping is, why it harms domestic producers, and what protection the importing country uses in response.
hints: Start with what the foreign exporter is doing to its price and why.
Link that pricing to the effect on domestic firms, then to the action the importing government takes.
questions.targets: Anti-dumping as a case for protection

questions.prompt: Veld used to import rice from Kuva, the lowest-cost producer in the world. After Veld joins a customs union with Tarn, it imports rice from Tarn instead, where rice costs more to produce. What is this an example of?

options.text: Trade creation
options.misconception: Trade creation is a switch towards a lower-cost producer, not a higher-cost one.

options.text: Trade diversion
Dumping
options.misconception: Dumping is selling exports below cost; nothing here says Tarn prices below its cost.

options.text: Comparative advantage
options.misconception: The switch is caused by the tariff arrangement, and moves trade away from the producer with the lower opportunity cost.

hints: Think about how joining a bloc changes which supplier is cheapest for Veld's importers.
Compare the production cost of the old and the new supplier and ask whether world resources are now used better or worse.

questions.prompt: Table 2 shows data for a steel firm in Kuva that exports to Veld. Calculate, as a percentage of average cost, how far the firm's export price is below its average cost.

table.caption: Table 2: Kuvan steel firm, 2025 (kuvars per tonne)

questions.model_answer_note: Correct working and 20% earns 2; correct answer with no working earns 1.
hints: Use the average cost and the export price from Table 2.
Find the gap between the two prices, divide by the average cost, then multiply by 100.
questions.targets: Evidence of dumping from cost data

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a common market and a monetary union.
marking_points: A common market has free trade, a common external tariff and free movement of labour and capital, but members keep their own currencies [1]
A monetary union adds a common currency and a single central bank / common monetary policy (and exchange rate) [1]
questions.model_answer_note: The answer must show what the two share and the extra feature of a monetary union; describing only one type earns 1.
hints: Place both on the stages of economic integration; one is the step after the other.
Say what a common market already includes, then state what members give up and share when they move one step further.
questions.targets: Asked as a comparison in past papers

questions.prompt: Explain how joining a common market could lead to a better use of factors of production in a member country.
marking_points: A common market allows free movement of labour and capital between members [1]
Workers can move to where there are jobs / skill shortages, and capital can flow to where its return is highest [1]
So resources move to their most productive uses, improving allocation and raising employment and output [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full answer names the free movement of factors, explains where they move, and links this to better resource allocation or employment.
hints: Think about which feature a common market adds beyond free trade in goods.
Follow what happens to unemployed workers and to spare capital when they can move across borders, then link to efficiency.

questions.prompt: Tarn places a tariff on imported shoes to protect jobs in its shoe industry. Which outcome is most likely to reduce the overall benefit of this policy for Tarn's workers?

options.text: Domestic shoe production in Tarn rises
options.misconception: This is the intended effect of the tariff, not a problem with it.

options.text: The government of Tarn collects tariff revenue
options.misconception: Revenue is a side benefit of the tariff.

options.text: Shoe imports into Tarn fall
options.misconception: Fewer imports is how the tariff protects domestic producers.

options.text: Trading partners respond with tariffs on Tarn's exports

hints: Think about how other countries might react to the tariff.
Trace what happens to Tarn's export industries, and their workers, if other countries react.
questions.targets: Retaliation as a cost of protection

questions.prompt: Table 3 shows Tarn's exports. Tarn joined the Coral trading bloc in 2020. By what percentage did Tarn's exports to other Coral members rise between 2019 and 2023?

options.misconception: This is the change in US$ billion, not a percentage change.
This divides the change by the 2023 value instead of the 2019 value.
This is roughly the share of Tarn's 2023 exports that went to Coral members.

hints: Use the percentage change formula on the row for Coral members.
Subtract the old value from the new, then divide by the old value and multiply by 100.

questions.prompt: Table 4 shows Veld's tariffs on imported cars. All five countries are WTO members, and Veld has no trade agreement with any of them. Which statement is correct?

table.caption: Table 4: Veld's tariffs on imported cars, 2025

options.text: Veld breaks WTO rules because it charges a tariff at all
options.misconception: WTO members may charge tariffs up to agreed limits; they do not have to remove all tariffs.

options.text: Veld breaks WTO rules because it treats imports from Ostra more favourably than imports from the others
Veld follows WTO rules because all its tariffs are below 15%
options.misconception: The level of a tariff is not the issue here; how different partners are treated is.

options.text: Veld breaks WTO rules because its tariffs on Kuva, Tarn and Rudd are the same
options.misconception: Charging members the same tariff is what WTO rules ask for.

hints: Use the WTO principle of non-discrimination (most-favoured nation).
Compare the tariff each partner faces and ask whether any member gets a better deal outside a trade agreement.

questions.prompt: Which is the most likely reason why a country would choose to join a common market rather than a free trade area?

options.text: To keep full control over its own tariffs on imports from non-members
options.misconception: A common market requires a common external tariff, so this control is given up.

options.text: To allow labour and capital to move to where they are most productive across member countries
To adopt a common currency with its trading partners
options.misconception: A common currency is a feature of a monetary union, not a common market.

options.text: To be allowed to keep tariffs on imports from other members
options.misconception: Tariffs between members are removed in both types of bloc.

hints: Think about what a common market offers that a free trade area does not.
Check each option against the features of a common market and ask which is a gain, not a loss.
questions.targets: Joining a common market: factor mobility

questions.prompt: Table 5 shows the market for bicycles in Veld with a tariff of US$20 per bicycle and after the tariff is removed. The world price is US$100. Calculate (a) the change in the quantity of bicycles imported and (b) the tariff revenue the government gives up by removing the tariff.

table.caption: Table 5: Market for bicycles in Veld

marking_points: (a) Imports with tariff = 50 − 20 = 30 thousand and without tariff = 60 − 12 = 48 thousand [1]
(a) Change = +18 thousand bicycles [1]
(b) Revenue given up = US$20 × 30 000 = US$600 000 [1]
questions.model_answer_note: Full marks need both import figures, the change of +18 thousand, and US$600 000 with working.
hints: Imports are the gap between quantity demanded and domestic quantity supplied; tariff revenue uses imports under the tariff.
Find imports in each column, subtract, then multiply the tariff per unit by the number of units imported while the tariff was in place.

questions.prompt: Explain how trade protection can lead to an inefficient allocation of resources.
marking_points: Protection shields domestic firms from lower-cost foreign competition [1]
So resources stay in (or move to) industries where the country does not have a comparative advantage / high-cost producers survive [1]
Firms have less incentive to cut costs or innovate, so output is produced at higher cost than necessary [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full answer links protection to reduced competition, to resources used where opportunity costs are high, and to weaker incentives for efficiency.
hints: Think about comparative advantage and what competition normally forces firms to do.
Follow what happens to high-cost domestic firms when imports are restricted, and where resources end up.

questions.prompt: Veld is in a monetary union. Veld goes into recession while the other members are growing fast. Which is the main problem Veld faces?

options.text: It must pay tariffs on its exports to other members
options.misconception: There are no tariffs between members of a monetary union.

options.text: Its workers cannot move to other member countries
options.misconception: Free movement of labour is part of a monetary union.

options.text: It cannot lower its own interest rates or let its own currency depreciate
It must charge a different tariff on non-members from the other members
options.misconception: Members share a common external tariff.

hints: Think about which economic policy tools a member gives up when it shares a currency.
Ask what Veld would normally do to boost demand in a recession, and whether it still controls those tools.
questions.targets: Cost of monetary union: loss of independent monetary policy

questions.prompt: Veld believes that Kuva is giving its exporters subsidies that break WTO rules. What can the WTO do?

options.text: Rule on the dispute and, if Kuva does not comply, allow Veld to impose retaliatory tariffs
Fine Kuva's government and pay the fine to Veld's firms
options.misconception: The WTO does not collect fines or pay compensation to firms.

options.text: Lend money to Veld's firms to make up their lost sales
options.misconception: The WTO is not a lender.

options.text: Remove Kuva's subsidies directly from its national budget
options.misconception: The WTO cannot change a member's budget; it can only rule and authorise responses.

hints: Think about the WTO's role when members disagree.
Ask which option matches the powers of an organization that sets and enforces trade rules but has no money or control over budgets.

questions.prompt: Veld joined a trading bloc in 2021. Table 6 shows Veld's imports. Calculate the share of Veld's total imports that came from bloc members in 2020 and in 2024.
questions.model_answer_note: One mark for each correct share with working.
hints: Total imports in each year are the two rows added together.
Divide imports from members by total imports for each year, then multiply by 100.

questions.prompt: Which criticism is often made of the WTO by developing countries?

options.text: The WTO sets exchange rates that favour developed countries
options.misconception: The WTO does not set exchange rates.

options.text: Developed countries keep subsidising their farmers while developing countries are pressed to open their markets
The WTO has no way of settling trade disputes
options.misconception: The WTO has a dispute settlement process.

options.text: The WTO only allows developed countries to become members
options.misconception: Most WTO members are developing countries.

hints: Think about the sectors where developing countries often have a comparative advantage.
Remove the options that are factually wrong about the WTO, then consider whose trade barriers have been hardest to reduce.

questions.prompt: Table 7 shows the cost of producing a tonne of rice in Kuva and in Tarn. Veld charges a 25% tariff on all rice imports and buys from the cheapest source. Veld then forms a customs union with Tarn and keeps a 25% tariff on non-members. (a) Calculate the price per tonne Veld's importers pay before and after the customs union. (b) State whether this change is trade creation or trade diversion.

table.caption: Table 7: Cost of producing rice (US$ per tonne, before any tariff)

marking_points: (a) Before: Kuva 80 × 1.25 = US$100 (Tarn would be 90 × 1.25 = US$112.50), so Veld pays US$100 [1]
(a) After: Tarn has no tariff, so US$90 (Kuva still US$100), so Veld pays US$90 [1]
(b) Trade diversion: imports switch from the lower-cost non-member (Kuva) to the higher-cost member (Tarn) [1]
questions.model_answer_note: Full marks need both prices with tariff working and the correct classification with a reason tied to production costs.
hints: Work out the tariff-inclusive price from each country, before and after Veld joins.
Pick the cheapest source in each case, then compare the production cost of the new supplier with that of the old one.
questions.targets: Trade creation vs diversion with numbers

questions.prompt: Rudd joined the WTO in 2010. Table 8 shows its average tariff rate. Calculate the percentage change in Rudd's average tariff rate between 2010 and 2025.
questions.model_answer_note: Correct working and −50% earns 2. An answer of 10 (percentage points) earns 0 for the result.
hints: Use the percentage change formula on the first and last years in Table 8.
The rates are already percentages, so treat them as the numbers in the formula; do not just subtract them.

questions.prompt: Explain one disadvantage for a country of joining a customs union.
marking_points: Disadvantage identified, e.g. loss of control over its own trade policy / must adopt the common external tariff [1]
Explanation, e.g. the country can no longer set tariffs to suit its own industries or sign separate trade deals with non-members [1]
Consequence, e.g. it may have to import from higher-cost members instead of cheaper non-members, raising prices / its protected industries may shrink and workers lose jobs [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full answer names one disadvantage, explains why joining causes it, and states who in the country loses.
hints: Think about what a member of a customs union must agree to on trade with countries outside the bloc.
Pick one cost, say why membership causes it, then say what it means for consumers, firms or workers.

questions.prompt: Explain two reasons why a government might remove a tariff on an imported good.
marking_points: Reason 1 identified, e.g. to lower prices for consumers / raise consumer surplus [1]
Reason 1 explained, e.g. without the tariff the domestic price falls to the world price, so consumers buy more at a lower price [1]
Reason 2 identified, e.g. to lower costs for domestic firms that use the import as an input / to improve efficiency / to meet trade agreement or WTO commitments / to avoid retaliation [1]
Reason 2 explained, e.g. cheaper inputs cut production costs and make domestic firms more competitive; or more competition forces domestic producers to become efficient [1]
questions.model_answer_note: Two separate reasons, each named and then linked to its effect, earn 4; two reasons named without explanation earn 2.
hints: Think about who gains when the domestic price falls to the world price, and about the country's trade commitments.
For each reason, name who benefits, then give the chain from lower import prices to that benefit.

questions.prompt: Explain why it can be difficult for WTO members to reach new multilateral trade agreements.
marking_points: Agreements need consensus among a very large number of member countries [1]
Members have different interests, e.g. developed countries want access for manufactures and services while developing countries want cuts in agricultural subsidies [1]
Domestic pressure groups / governments resist removing protection for their own industries, so talks stall [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full answer links the number of members and the decision rule to conflicting interests and domestic political pressure.
hints: Think about how many countries negotiate and how decisions are made.
Give an example of two groups of members wanting different things, then add why governments at home find it hard to give way.
questions.targets: Limits of the WTO in negotiations
